concept.name: Par yield
concept.definition: The coupon rate at which a hypothetical bond of a given maturity would price exactly at par (100% of face value), given the current discount function. The U.S. Treasury's official daily yield curve is a par yield curve, and its constant-maturity (CMT) rates are par yields read from that curve.
concept.intuition: It is the coupon a brand-new bond of a given maturity would have to pay today for investors to accept it at full face value.
concept.mechanics: Treasury converts indicative bid-side price quotations on the most recently auctioned securities to yields, bootstraps forward rates, and applies monotone convex interpolation to construct a curve of true par rates; CMT yields are then read at fixed maturities and quoted as semiannual bond-equivalent yields.
concept.formula: Par coupon c solves 100 = Σ_t (c/2) × DF(t) + 100 × DF(T), where DF(t) are discount factors and T is maturity (semiannual coupons).
concept.failure_modes: CMT par yields are read from a fitted curve and may not match the actual yield of any specific traded security; the curve also depends on the fitting methodology, which Treasury has changed over time.
concept.misconceptions: A par yield is not the same as the spot rate for that maturity, and a CMT rate is not the yield on an actual outstanding bond of exactly that maturity.
concept.example: If the fitted 10-year par yield is 4.30%, a new theoretical 10-year bond with a 4.30% coupon would be worth exactly 100.
